question: Which chamber of the heart receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins?
explanation: The left atrium receives freshly oxygenated blood directly from the lungs via the four pulmonary veins before passing it to the left ventricle. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is the muscular wall of the left ventricle significantly thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?

options.A: It contracts at a much faster rhythm than the right side
options.B: It receives blood directly under high pressure from the lungs
options.C: It pumps blood through the high-resistance systemic circulation
options.D: It holds a larger total volume of blood at any given time

explanation: The left ventricle requires a heavier musculature to generate the high pressures necessary to circulate blood throughout the entire body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h1)

question: What is the primary function of the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles?

options.A: Initiating the electrical action potential in the sinoatrial node
options.B: Preventing the atrioventricular valves from prolapsing into the atria
options.C: Opening the semilunar valves during ventricular diastole
options.D: Regulating the systemic blood pressure during exercise

explanation: Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles anchor the AV valves securely, stopping them from swinging backward into the atria when ventricular pressure rises. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which of the following structures is NOT a heart valve?
explanation: The superior and inferior venae cavae empty directly into the right atrium without a formal anatomical valve. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h2)

question: Where do the coronary arteries directly originate from?
explanation: The coronary arteries branch off from the ascending aorta immediately distal to the aortic semilunar valve. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h3)

question: A blockage in the coronary sinus would most directly impair the return of deoxygenated blood from where?
explanation: The coronary sinus collects venous blood exclusively from the heart muscle tissue and drains it into the right atrium. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is known as the natural pacemaker of the heart?
explanation: The sinoatrial node generates electrical impulses at the fastest rate, establishing the basic rhythm of normal cardiac contractions. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is the functional significance of the electrical delay that occurs at the atrioventricular node?

options.A: It ensures that blood flows backward into the vena cava during periods of rest
options.B: It allows the atria time to contract and empty blood into the ventricles before ventricular contraction begins
options.C: It gives the SA node time to recharge its electrolyte balance between consecutive heartbeats
options.D: It protects the delicate heart tissue from receiving dangerously high voltages during physical exertion

explanation: The brief pause at the AV node ensures mechanical efficiency by making sure atrial chambers finish pumping blood downward before the ventricles squeeze. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h4)

question: What physiological event causes the first heart sound, often described as 'lub'?

options.C: Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves

explanation: The closure of the tricuspid and mitral valves at the start of ventricular systole produces the lower-pitched first heart sound. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h5)

question: During which specific phase of the cardiac cycle are both the atrioventricular and semilunar valves closed at the same time?
explanation: Immediately after ventricular contraction begins, pressure rises, closing the AV valves while semilunar valves have not yet opened, resulting in a brief period where blood volume is constant with all valves closed. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h5)

question: How is cardiac output calculated?

options.A: Stroke volume divided by blood pressure
options.C: Heart rate divided by total peripheral resistance
options.D: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume

explanation: Cardiac output equals the number of beats per minute multiplied by the volume of blood pumped during each individual contraction. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h6)

question: An increase in parasympathetic nerve activity directed at the heart will result in which of the following?

options.A: A decrease in coronary blood flow

explanation: Parasympathetic input through the vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, which hyperpolarizes the SA node and reduces the heart rate. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h6)

question: What physiological process does the QRS complex on an ECG represent?
explanation: The prominent QRS complex corresponds to the electrical depolarization sweeping through the muscular ventricles prior to their contraction. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h7)

question: Why is atrial repolarization typically not visible on a standard surface ECG tracing?

options.A: Skin electrodes are positioned too far from the atria to detect small voltage changes
options.B: It is completely absorbed by the insulating layer of the fibrous pericardium
options.C: It occurs at the exact same time as the much larger QRS complex, masking the wave
options.D: The atria do not actually undergo electrical repolarization after contraction

explanation: The electrical activity of atrial repolarization is buried within and overshadowed by the high-voltage QRS complex representing ventricular depolarization. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T4#GNS111_U2_T4_h7)
